To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cytoplasmically located domain of the influenza hemagglutini is not required for the expression of a bioloically active molecule at the cell surface and that mutations in this region can alter the rate at which the protein moves from the endoplamic reticulum to its final destination, the plasma membrane.
mutations in the cytoplamic domain of the influenza HA molecule affect different stages of its intracellular transport.

mutations in the cytoplamic domain of the HA protein can affect different steps of its intracellular transport and that the cytoplasmatic domain is not absolutely required for efficient expression of a functional HA protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which influenza virus hemagluttinin is transported from the endoplamic reticulum to its final location on the cell surface.
the mechanisms of intracellular transport of influenza virus proteins and the effects of mutations in the viral genome on the transport process.

the role of specific regions of the influenza virus HA in the process of transport from the ER to the cell surface and with the effect of mutations in these regions on the biological activity of the protein.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cytoplasmatic domain of HA plays an important role in intracellular transport of the protein.
the cytoplasmatic domain is involved in intracellular transport of HA but that it does not seem to be the sole determinant.
the cytoplasm tail of HA plays an important role in the transport process, but is not absolutely essential for transport.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mutations in the cytoplamic domain of HA can affect the rate of intracelluar transport of HA, and the efficiency with whch HA reaches the cell surace.
the HA cytoplasmic region is important for efficient transport of HA from the endoplamic reticulum to plasma membrane, but is not required for the biological activity of the protein.

the HA cytoplasmic tail is not essential for the transport and expression of HA on the cell surface, and that mutations in the cytoplamic tail do not always result in a loss of function of HA, but can result in a change in function of HA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HA cytoplasmic tail is a critical determinant of intracellular transport of HA.

the cytoplasmically exposed region of HA is not required for the transport of the molecule from the endoplamic reticulum to cell surface, and the mutations in this region did not alter the biological activity of the molecule.
there are multiple mechanisms that can lead to the expression of HA on the surface, and that these mechanisms can be differentially used by influenza viruses.
